topics.name: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
topics.summary: This topic covers the most direct application of definite integrals to area: the region enclosed by a single curve \( y=f(x) \), the \( x \)-axis (or, symmetrically, \( x=g(y) \) and the \( y \)-axis), and one or two boundary lines. When the curve stays on one side of the axis, the area is simply \( \int_a^b y\,dx \) (or \( \int_c^d x\,dy \)). The main difficulty arises when the curve crosses the axis inside the interval: the raw integral then mixes a positive contribution with a negative one and can cancel to a small or even negative number, which is never a valid area. The fix is to locate every point where the curve meets the axis, split the integral there, take the absolute value of any piece below the axis, and add the pieces. Recognising whether a region is naturally bounded by the \( x \)-axis (integrate in \( x \)) or the \( y \)-axis (integrate in \( y \)) is also part of this topic, since the wrong choice leads to awkward or incorrect bounds.
key_formulas: \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_a^b y\,dx \), for a region bounded by \( y=f(x) \) and the \( x \)-axis
\( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_c^d x\,dy \), for a region bounded by \( x=g(y) \) and the \( y \)-axis
If \( f \) changes sign at \( x=k \) inside \( [a,b] \): \( \text{Area} = \left|\displaystyle\int_a^k f\,dx\right| + \left|\displaystyle\int_k^b f\,dx\right| \)
topics.worked_example: Find the area bounded by \( y=x^2 \), the \( x \)-axis, \( x=0 \), and \( x=3 \). Since \( x^2\ge0 \) throughout, no splitting is needed: \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_0^3 x^2\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = 9 \) sq. units.
common_mistakes: Reporting the raw signed value of the definite integral as the area when the curve dips below the axis inside the interval, instead of splitting and taking absolute values
Failing to notice that the curve crosses the axis inside the given bounds, and so never splitting the integral at all
Integrating with respect to the wrong variable — using \( dx \) for a region that is naturally bounded by the \( y \)-axis, or vice versa

topics.name: Area Between Two Curves (Intersection Points and Bounded Regions)
topics.summary: This topic extends the idea of area to the region enclosed between two curves \( y=f(x) \) and \( y=g(x) \), rather than between one curve and an axis. The first step is always to find the intersection points by solving \( f(x)=g(x) \); these become the limits of integration (or, if the region is also naturally bounded by given vertical lines, those lines combine with the intersection points to fix the interval). Once the interval is fixed, the area is \( \int(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,dx \), where \"upper\" and \"lower\" must be determined by checking which function has the larger value on that interval — not simply assumed from the order the functions were written in the problem. The topic becomes more demanding when the two curves cross three or more times within the region of interest: the curve that is \"upper\" on one sub-interval may become \"lower\" on the next, so the integral must be split at every interior intersection point, with the subtraction order re-checked (and reversed if necessary) on each piece before the pieces are added together.
key_formulas: \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_a^b \bigl[f(x)-g(x)\bigr]\,dx \), where \( f \) is upper and \( g \) is lower on \( [a,b] \), and \( a,b \) are intersection points
With an interior crossing at \( x=k \): \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_a^k[f-g]\,dx + \int_k^b[g-f]\,dx \) (subtraction order reverses across \( k \))
topics.worked_example: Find the area between \( y=x^2 \) and \( y=x+2 \). Solving \( x^2=x+2 \) gives \( x=-1,2 \); checking \( x=0 \) shows the line is upper. \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{-1}^2\bigl[(x+2)-x^2\bigr]dx = \dfrac{9}{2} \) sq. units.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the two functions in a fixed order throughout, without checking (and re-checking on each sub-interval) which one is actually upper
Missing an interior intersection point when the two curves cross three or more times, so one sub-interval uses the wrong pair of curves
Solving for intersection points but forgetting to also incorporate any vertical lines the problem explicitly gives as boundaries

topics.name: Area of Standard Curves: Circle, Parabola, and Ellipse
topics.summary: This topic applies the general area-by-integration method to the three standard conics of the syllabus — circles \( x^2+y^2=a^2 \), parabolas such as \( y^2=4ax \), and ellipses \( \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1 \) — and to natural sub-regions of them such as a quadrant, a half, or the area cut off by a latus rectum or a vertical chord. The key technical tool is the standard antiderivative \( \int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx = \dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+\dfrac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{a} \), which appears whenever a circle or ellipse boundary is integrated directly; recognising standard angles such as \( \sin^{-1}(1/2)=\pi/6 \) keeps the results clean. For a vertical chord \( x=c \) cutting off the region between \( x=c \) and \( x=a \), the area works out to \( a^2\cos^{-1}(c/a) - c\sqrt{a^2-c^2} \) for a circle, with an extra factor of \( b/a \) for an ellipse of semi-axes \( a,b \) — both boundary terms of the antiderivative are needed, and it is easy to keep only the inverse-trigonometric term and forget the algebraic correction term.
key_formulas: Circle \( x^2+y^2=a^2 \): full area \( \pi a^2 \); one quadrant \( \dfrac{\pi a^2}{4} \)
Parabola \( y^2=4ax \) cut off by its latus rectum \( x=a \): area \( \dfrac{8a^2}{3} \)
Circle segment to the right of chord \( x=c \): \( a^2\cos^{-1}\dfrac{c}{a} - c\sqrt{a^2-c^2} \) (multiply by \( b/a \) for the corresponding ellipse segment)
topics.worked_example: Find the area inside \( x^2+y^2=4 \) and to the right of \( x=1 \). Since \( a=2 \) and \( \sin^{-1}(1/2)=\pi/6 \), \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_1^2 2\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3} \) sq. units.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to subtract the algebraic correction term \( c\sqrt{a^2-c^2} \) and reporting only the inverse-trigonometric part of the antiderivative
Treating an ellipse exactly like a circle of radius \( a \), ignoring the semi-minor axis \( b \) and the resulting \( b/a \) scaling factor
Forgetting that the full vertical extent at a given \( x \) is \( 2\sqrt{a^2-x^2} \) (both halves), not just \( \sqrt{a^2-x^2} \)

topics.name: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
topics.summary: This topic focuses on the region enclosed between a curve — typically a parabola or a low-degree polynomial — and a straight line that is not simply the \( x \)-axis. The method is the same upper-minus-lower integration used for two general curves: solve the curve's equation together with the line's equation to find the true intersection points, determine which of the two is upper on the interval between them, and integrate the difference. A frequent trap is to use a convenient but irrelevant number — such as the curve's own \( x \)-intercept, or the line's own \( x \)-intercept — as an integration bound instead of actually solving the two equations together. At the higher end of this topic, the curve can be a cubic that meets the line at three rational points; here the line and curve trade places as \"upper\" partway through, so the integral must be split at the interior intersection point exactly as in the two-curves topic, with the subtraction order re-checked on each piece.
key_formulas: \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_a^b\bigl[(\text{line or curve, whichever is upper})-(\text{the other})\bigr]dx \), where \( a,b \) solve curve \( = \) line
For \( y=x^2+\dots \) meeting a line at two points with gap \( g \): \( \text{Area} = \dfrac{g^3}{6} \) (scale by the leading coefficient if it isn't \( 1 \))
topics.worked_example: Find the area between \( y=x^2 \) and \( y=3x-2 \). Solving \( x^2=3x-2 \) gives \( x=1,2 \); the line is upper. \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_1^2\bigl[(3x-2)-x^2\bigr]dx = \dfrac{1}{6} \) sq. units.
common_mistakes: Using the curve's or the line's own \( x \)-intercept as an integration bound, instead of solving the curve and line simultaneously for the true intersection points
Subtracting curve minus line (or line minus curve) by fixed habit, without checking which one is actually upper on the interval
When the curve is a cubic meeting the line at three points, failing to split at the interior intersection and re-check the subtraction order there

topics.name: Area Involving Symmetry, Modulus, and Piecewise/Multi-Region Curves
topics.summary: This topic gathers three closely related ideas that all complicate a basic area integral: absolute values (modulus), symmetry, and piecewise-defined curves. For a region bounded by \( y=|f(x)| \), the correct approach is to find every point where \( f(x)=0 \) inside the interval, split the integral there, and on each piece integrate \( f \) or \( -f \) according to its sign — never the raw, un-modulused \( f \) directly, which can understate the area or even give a nonsensical negative or cancelled result. Symmetry — about the \( y \)-axis for an even function, or the fourfold symmetry of a figure such as \( |x|+|y|=a \) — is a shortcut for exactly these split-integral computations: find the area of one representative piece (a half or a quadrant) and multiply, rather than integrating over the whole region directly. Piecewise-defined functions require the same discipline as splitting for modulus: each formula in the definition applies only on its own sub-interval, and a region spanning two or three pieces needs a separate integral — with the correct formula — for each one.
key_formulas: \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_a^b |f(x)|\,dx \): split at each zero of \( f \) inside \( [a,b] \), integrating \( f \) where it's positive and \( -f \) where it's negative
Even function, symmetric about the \( y \)-axis: \( \text{Area} = 2\displaystyle\int_0^a |f(x)|\,dx \)
topics.worked_example: Find the area bounded by \( y=|x-2| \), the \( x \)-axis, \( x=0 \), and \( x=5 \). The sign change is at \( x=2 \): \( \text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_0^2(2-x)\,dx + \int_2^5(x-2)\,dx = 2+\dfrac{9}{2} = \dfrac{13}{2} \) sq. units.
common_mistakes: Dropping the absolute value and integrating the raw expression directly across the whole interval, which can understate the area or make positive and negative pieces cancel
Using symmetry to compute the area of only one half (or one quadrant) of a symmetric figure and forgetting to multiply by \( 2 \) (or \( 4 \))
In a piecewise-defined function, applying one piece's formula across the entire interval instead of switching to the correct formula at each breakpoint

questions.topic: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve \( y = x^2 \), the \( x \)-axis, and the ordinates \( x = 0 \) and \( x = 2 \).
questions.explanation:
The required area is \( \displaystyle\int_0^2 x^2\,dx \).

Integrating, \( \displaystyle\int_0^2 x^2\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{8}{3} - 0 = \dfrac{8}{3} \).

Since \( y = x^2 \ge 0 \) on \( [0,2] \), the curve never dips below the \( x \)-axis here, so no sign correction is needed and \( \dfrac{8}{3} \) sq. units is already the geometric area.
questions.hint: Set up \( \int_0^2 x^2\,dx \) and apply the power rule for integration carefully.
distractor_logic: used \( x^2/2 \) as the antiderivative of \( x^2 \) instead of \( x^3/3 \), forgetting to raise the power by one before dividing
read off the ordinate of the curve at \( x = 2 \) (which is \( y = 4 \)) and reported that value itself as the area
correctly raised the limit to \( x^3 \) but forgot to divide by the new power 3 before substituting the limits

questions.topic: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
questions.question: Find the area bounded by the curve \( y = x^3 \), the \( x \)-axis, and the lines \( x = 0 \), \( x = 2 \).
questions.explanation:
The required area is \( \displaystyle\int_0^2 x^3\,dx \).

\( \displaystyle\int_0^2 x^3\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{16}{4} - 0 = 4 \).

The curve lies entirely on or above the \( x \)-axis on \( [0,2] \), so \( 4 \) sq. units is the actual area, with no sign correction needed.
questions.hint: Integrate \( x^3 \) using the power rule and substitute the limits \( 0 \) and \( 2 \).
distractor_logic: used denominator 3 (the power rule for \( x^2 \)) instead of 4 when writing the antiderivative of \( x^3 \)
evaluated the ordinate \( y(2) = 8 \) and reported that height as the area instead of integrating
correctly raised the power to \( x^4 \) but forgot to divide by the new power 4 before substituting the limits

questions.topic: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the line \( y = 3x + 2 \), the \( x \)-axis, and the ordinates \( x = 0 \) and \( x = 4 \).
questions.explanation:
The required area is \( \displaystyle\int_0^4 (3x+2)\,dx \).

\( \displaystyle\int_0^4 (3x+2)\,dx = \left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2} + 2x\right]_0^4 = (24 + 8) - 0 = 32 \).

Since \( y = 3x+2 > 0 \) throughout \( [0,4] \), this value is already the geometric area.
questions.hint: This is a trapezoid under a line — integrate \( 3x+2 \) directly rather than guessing a triangle formula.
distractor_logic: integrated only the \( 3x \) term and dropped the constant term \( 2 \) from the antiderivative
evaluated the function at \( x = 4 \) (getting \( y = 14 \)) and reported that ordinate as the area instead of integrating
treated the region as a right triangle using half of the base times the endpoint height \( 14 \), ignoring the trapezoidal shape caused by the non-zero \( y \)-intercept

questions.topic: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the line \( y = 4 - x \), the \( x \)-axis, and the ordinate \( x = 0 \), up to the point where the line meets the \( x \)-axis.
questions.explanation:
The line meets the \( x \)-axis where \( 4-x=0 \), i.e. \( x=4 \). The required area is \( \displaystyle\int_0^4 (4-x)\,dx \).

\( \displaystyle\int_0^4 (4-x)\,dx = \left[4x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^4 = (16-8)-0 = 8 \).

The line lies above the \( x \)-axis throughout \( [0,4] \), so \( 8 \) sq. units is already the correct area — a sign slip in the integrand is the only way to land on a negative value here.
questions.hint: First find where the line crosses the \( x \)-axis, then integrate \( 4-x \) up to that point.
distractor_logic: made a sign slip while integrating, evaluating \( \int_0^4 (x-4)\,dx \) instead of \( \int_0^4 (4-x)\,dx \), and reported the resulting negative number directly as the area
used the full rectangle of width 4 and height 4 (the \( y \)-intercept) instead of recognising the region is a triangle
misread the \( x \)-intercept as \( x = 2 \) instead of \( x = 4 \) and integrated only up to that wrong upper limit

questions.topic: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve \( y = x^2 \), the \( y \)-axis, and the lines \( y = 0 \) and \( y = 4 \).
questions.explanation:
Since the region is bounded by the \( y \)-axis, integrate with respect to \( y \), using \( x = \sqrt{y} \).

Area \( = \displaystyle\int_0^4 x\,dy = \int_0^4 y^{1/2}\,dy = \left[\dfrac{2}{3}y^{3/2}\right]_0^4 = \dfrac{2}{3}(8) - 0 = \dfrac{16}{3} \).

The curve lies to the right of the \( y \)-axis throughout, so \( \dfrac{16}{3} \) sq. units is the correct area with no sign issue.
questions.hint: Rewrite \( y=x^2 \) as \( x=\sqrt{y} \) first, since the boundary here is the \( y \)-axis, so you integrate with respect to \( y \).
distractor_logic: integrated with respect to \( x \) instead of \( y \), using \( \int_0^2 x^2\,dx \) even though the region is bounded by the \( y \)-axis
rewrote \( y = x^2 \) incorrectly as \( x = y \) (a straight line) instead of \( x = \sqrt{y} \) before integrating with respect to \( y \)
found the boundary value \( x = \sqrt{4} = 2 \) and reported that ordinate as the area instead of integrating

questions.topic: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve \( y = 2x^2 \), the \( x \)-axis, and the ordinates \( x = 0 \) and \( x = 2 \).
questions.explanation:
The required area is \( \displaystyle\int_0^2 2x^2\,dx \).

\( \displaystyle\int_0^2 2x^2\,dx = \left[\dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{16}{3} - 0 = \dfrac{16}{3} \).

Since \( y \ge 0 \) throughout \( [0,2] \), \( \dfrac{16}{3} \) sq. units is already the geometric area.
questions.hint: Keep the coefficient \( 2 \) attached throughout the integration — it's easy to drop while applying the power rule.

questions.topic: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
questions.question: Find the area of the triangle bounded by the line \( y = x \), the \( x \)-axis, and the ordinate \( x = 5 \), by using integration.
questions.explanation:
Area \( = \displaystyle\int_0^5 x\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^5 = \dfrac{25}{2} - 0 = \dfrac{25}{2} \).

This matches the elementary triangle-area check: half of base \( 5 \) times height \( 5 \) also gives \( \dfrac{25}{2} \), confirming the integral.
questions.hint: This region is a right triangle — integrate \( y=x \) from \( 0 \) to \( 5 \), or cross-check with half of base times height.
distractor_logic: used the full rectangle (base \( \times \) height \( = 5 \times 5 \)) instead of accounting for the triangular shape under the line
reported the height of the line at \( x = 5 \) as the area instead of integrating
used \( x^2/3 \) instead of \( x^2/2 \) as the antiderivative of \( x \), confusing the power-rule denominator

questions.topic: Area Under a Simple Curve Bounded by the X-axis or Y-axis
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve \( y = x^3 \), the \( y \)-axis, and the lines \( y = 0 \) and \( y = 8 \).
questions.explanation:
Since \( y=x^3 \) gives \( x=y^{1/3} \), and the region is bounded by the \( y \)-axis, integrate with respect to \( y \).

Area \( = \displaystyle\int_0^8 y^{1/3}\,dy = \left[\dfrac{3}{4}y^{4/3}\right]_0^8 = \dfrac{3}{4}(16) - 0 = 12 \), using \( 8^{4/3} = (8^{1/3})^4 = 2^4 = 16 \).
questions.hint: Rewrite \( y=x^3 \) as \( x=y^{1/3} \) and integrate with respect to \( y \), since the \( y \)-axis is the bounding line.

questions.topic: Area Between Two Curves (Intersection Points and Bounded Regions)
questions.question: Find the area of the region enclosed between the curves \( y = x^2 \) and \( y = 4x - x^2 \).
questions.explanation:
Solve \( x^2 = 4x-x^2 \Rightarrow 2x^2-4x=0 \Rightarrow x=0,2 \), the true intersection points.

On \( (0,2) \), checking \( x=1 \): \( 4x-x^2=3 \) lies above \( x^2=1 \), so \( y=4x-x^2 \) is the upper curve.

Area \( = \displaystyle\int_0^2 \left[(4x-x^2)-x^2\right]dx = \int_0^2(4x-2x^2)\,dx = \left[2x^2-\dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = 8-\dfrac{16}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3} \) sq. units.
questions.hint: Solve \( x^2=4x-x^2 \) to get the true intersection points before setting up the integral — don't use where either curve meets the \( x \)-axis.
distractor_logic: subtracted in the wrong order, computing \( \int_0^2 \left(x^2-(4x-x^2)\right)dx \) (lower minus upper) instead of upper minus lower, and reported the resulting negative value directly
used \( x=4 \) (where \( y=4x-x^2 \) meets the \( x \)-axis) as the upper limit instead of solving \( x^2=4x-x^2 \) for the actual second intersection point \( x=2 \)
integrated only the upper curve \( y=4x-x^2 \) over \( [0,2] \) and forgot to subtract the lower curve \( y=x^2 \)

questions.topic: Area Between Two Curves (Intersection Points and Bounded Regions)
questions.question: Find the area of the region enclosed between the curves \( y = x^2 \) and \( y = -x^2+6x-4 \).
questions.explanation:
Solve \( x^2 = -x^2+6x-4 \Rightarrow 2x^2-6x+4=0 \Rightarrow x^2-3x+2=0 \Rightarrow x=1,2 \).

Checking \( x=1.5 \): \( -x^2+6x-4=2.75 \) lies above \( x^2=2.25 \), so \( y=-x^2+6x-4 \) is the upper curve on \( (1,2) \).

Area \( = \displaystyle\int_1^2\left[(-x^2+6x-4)-x^2\right]dx = \int_1^2(-2x^2+6x-4)\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{2x^3}{3}+3x^2-4x\right]_1^2 = \dfrac13 \) sq. units.
questions.hint: Solve the two equations simultaneously to get both true intersection points — don't assume the region starts where one curve happens to touch the origin.

used \( x=0 \) (where \( y=x^2 \) touches the origin) as the lower limit instead of solving \( x^2=-x^2+6x-4 \) for the actual first intersection point \( x=1 \)

questions.topic: Area Between Two Curves (Intersection Points and Bounded Regions)
questions.question: Find the area of the region enclosed between the curves \( y = x^2 - 4x \) and \( y = -x^2 + 4x \).
questions.explanation:
Solve \( x^2-4x = -x^2+4x \Rightarrow 2x^2-8x=0 \Rightarrow x=0,4 \), the intersection points.

Checking \( x=2 \): \( -x^2+4x=4 \) lies above \( x^2-4x=-4 \), so \( y=-x^2+4x \) is the upper curve on \( (0,4) \).

Area \( = \displaystyle\int_0^4\left[(-x^2+4x)-(x^2-4x)\right]dx = \int_0^4(-2x^2+8x)\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{2x^3}{3}+4x^2\right]_0^4 = \dfrac{64}{3} \) sq. units.
questions.hint: The two parabolas are mirror images of each other about \( y=0 \) — find both intersection points and integrate the full difference over the whole interval.

questions.topic: Area Between Two Curves (Intersection Points and Bounded Regions)
questions.question: Find the area of the region enclosed between the curves \( y = x^2 - 9 \) and \( y = 9 - x^2 \).
questions.explanation:
Solve \( x^2-9=9-x^2 \Rightarrow 2x^2=18 \Rightarrow x=\pm3 \), the intersection points.

On \( (-3,3) \), \( y=9-x^2 \) lies above \( y=x^2-9 \) (check \( x=0 \): \( 9 \) vs \( -9 \)).

Area \( = \displaystyle\int_{-3}^3\left[(9-x^2)-(x^2-9)\right]dx = \int_{-3}^3(18-2x^2)\,dx = \left[18x-\dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{-3}^3 = 72 \) sq. units.
questions.hint: The region is symmetric about the \( y \)-axis — you can integrate over \( [0,3] \) and double the result, but remember to actually double it.

computed the area only over the right half \( [0,3] \), using the symmetry of the figure about \( x=0 \), but forgot to double the result

questions.topic: Area Between Two Curves (Intersection Points and Bounded Regions)
questions.question: Find the area of the region enclosed between the curves \( y = 2x^2 - 4x \) and \( y = -2x^2 + 4x \).
questions.explanation:
Solve \( 2x^2-4x=-2x^2+4x \Rightarrow 4x^2-8x=0 \Rightarrow x=0,2 \).

On \( (0,2) \), \( y=-2x^2+4x \) lies above \( y=2x^2-4x \) (check \( x=1 \): \( 2 \) vs \( -2 \)).

Area \( = \displaystyle\int_0^2\left[(-2x^2+4x)-(2x^2-4x)\right]dx = \int_0^2(-4x^2+8x)\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{4x^3}{3}+4x^2\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{16}{3} \) sq. units.
questions.hint: Find both intersection points first, decide which curve is on top between them, then integrate the difference over the full interval.

questions.topic: Area Between Two Curves (Intersection Points and Bounded Regions)
